entries.note: Prosody is usually preserved in the audio path and decodable in late LLM states yet only partially expressed in the final response, locating the bottleneck in using prosody rather than perceiving it; a single edit at the relevant layer often shifts the decision, though recovery is directional rather than a clean class restoration.

entries.name: RAIL
entries.full_title: RAIL: Rethinking Auditory Intelligence in Large Audio-Language Models with a CHC-Grounded Benchmark
entries.summary: A human-centric evaluation paradigm for large audio-language models grounded in the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) cognitive framework. RAIL formalises auditory cognition into five core capabilities and turns them into structured tasks probing how models process, retain and integrate auditory information, with principled data curation and human-aligned evaluation protocols, moving evaluation from task-level scores toward cognitive behaviours.
entries.note: Across 26 state-of-the-art LALMs, performance is highly uneven across the cognitive abilities.

entries.name: RedVox
entries.full_title: RedVox: Safety and Fairness Gaps in Speech Models Across Languages
entries.summary: A multilingual safety and fairness benchmark for speech-capable models built from real human voice recordings, covering unsafe requests and unfair stereotypical requests across five languages. The paper also surveys safety reporting practices in state-of-the-art speech model releases and documents the privacy challenges of collecting speech data from human participants.
entries.note: Only 8% of surveyed speech model releases document any multilingual safety analysis; across eight models vulnerabilities persist even non-adversarially, worsen outside English, and are amplified when the request is spoken rather than written.

entries.name: SpeechEditBench
entries.full_title: SpeechEditBench: A Bilingual Multi-Attribute Benchmark for Instruction-Guided Speech Editing
entries.summary: A bilingual multi-attribute benchmark for instruction-guided speech editing, covering seven atomic editing tasks plus compositional tasks that combine several operations in one instruction. An anchor-based protocol separately scores edit success on targeted attributes and preservation of untargeted ones, yielding target-success, preservation-success, and joint-success metrics.
entries.size: seven atomic editing tasks plus compositional tasks

entries.name: SpeechEQ
entries.full_title: SpeechEQ: Benchmarking Emotional Intelligence Quotient in Socially Aware Voice Conversational Models
entries.summary: A framework for evaluating the sociolinguistic and emotional reasoning of speech-language models in active multi-turn spoken dialogue, rather than through isolated text or passive acoustic perception. It provides a validated dialogue dataset organized by EQ-i 2.0 emotional-quotient subscales together with a multi-turn protocol scored by a proposed Spoken EQ (SEQ) score modeled on human EQ assessments.
entries.note: End-to-end architectures beat cascaded ones, but all models are bottlenecked by a text-reliant modality shortcut, an alignment-induced safety trap, and contextual amnesia.

entries.name: SpeechJBB
entries.full_title: SpeechJBB: Probing Safety Alignment and Comprehension in Large Audio Language Models under Code-Switched Speech
entries.summary: An audio jailbreak dataset for probing safety alignment of large audio language models beyond monolingual text prompts, focusing on code-switched harmful speech. An augmented setting inserts phonologically plausible pseudo-words around safety-critical terms to simulate localized obfuscation, testing whether natural-sounding perturbation bypasses safety policies.
languages: multilingual (code-switched; specific languages not given in the abstract)
entries.note: Code-switched harmful audio yields substantially higher jailbreak success, with non-English monolingual and non-English code-switched pairs the most vulnerable; pseudo-word insertion further lowers refusal rates.

entries.name: ST-AudioQA
entries.full_title: Spatio-Temporal Audio Language Modeling for Dynamic Sound Sources
entries.summary: A spatio-temporal audio question-answering dataset and benchmark built from first-order ambisonic renderings of static and moving sound sources. Each scene supplies source identity, activity, direction, distance and motion metadata, enabling questions about what is sounding, where it is, how it moves, and how sources relate; the paper also proposes an ST-Audio Encoder and ST-AudioLM that connects its audio tokens to an LLM.
tasks: direction, distance and motion trajectory questions

entries.name: StanceBench
entries.full_title: StanceBench: A Benchmark for Audio LLM-Based Interpersonal Stance Evaluation from Speech
entries.summary: A benchmark for measuring interpersonal stance in conversational speech and for testing audio-capable LLMs as automated stance judges. Built on the Seamless Interaction corpus, it specifies nine stance dimensions via role-prompt poles, standardises single-speaker and interaction-based evaluation, and reports LLM-as-a-judge robustness, bias and stance inference. Empathy and politeness are easiest; honesty is hardest and shows high prompt-order bias, while interaction stances are more context-sensitive with high variance.
entries.note: Honesty is the hardest stance and shows strong prompt-order bias, consistent with it needing cross-turn evidence.

entries.name: STEB
entries.full_title: STEB: A Speech-to-Speech Translation Expressiveness Benchmark for Evaluating Beyond Translation Fidelity
entries.summary: A 32.6-hour Chinese-English speech-to-speech translation benchmark that scores expressiveness preservation alongside standard dimensions (translation fidelity, speaker similarity, duration alignment). Expressiveness (emotion, scenario style, nonverbal vocalisations) is evaluated reference-free via a caption-then-summarize pipeline that turns speech into structured attributes and compares source and hypothesis with an LLM judge; human validation shows significant correlation with listener judgments. Six systems are evaluated, covering cascaded, end-to-end and speech large language models.
entries.note: Systems with strong translation fidelity, especially cascaded ones, still fail on emotion (best 3.82/5) and nonverbal-vocalization preservation (best 2.31/5).

entries.name: Voice AI Emotional Intelligence Gap
entries.full_title: Real-Time Voice AI Hears but Does Not Listen
entries.summary: An evaluation of four production real-time voice systems (GPT Realtime 2, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Qwen3.5 Omni Plus and Omni Flash) on scenarios where the words and the vocal delivery carry conflicting or complementary meaning. Three consequential scenarios test whether systems act on delivery, and separate probes test whether the same systems can identify the distress, fear or sarcasm they ignore when acting, plus accent and age estimation.
entries.note: All four systems act on the transcript rather than the voice — ending calls with crying callers, approving wire transfers spoken in frightened voices, enrolling sarcastic agreement — yet three of four can name the emotion when asked directly; prompting them to attend to delivery only partially and inconsistently helps.

entries.name: ESCUCHA
entries.full_title: ESCUCHA: A Spanish Speech Benchmark for Heterogeneous Acoustic Conditions
entries.summary: A Spanish speech-understanding benchmark for large audio language models under heterogeneous, real-world acoustic conditions. It comprises 1,000 human-curated questions paired with 162.9 hours of audio sourced from the wild rather than from existing datasets, with clips from a few seconds to over 80 minutes, spanning 9 perceptual and 10 reasoning categories, multiple Spanish accents and non-normative speech. It also includes multi-audio questions, spoken questions and audio instructions, and flags which questions support open-ended evaluation.
entries.io: audio in, text out (questions also given as speech)
entries.note: State-of-the-art multimodal and speech models fall substantially short of trained humans.

entries.name: FriendBench
entries.full_title: FriendBench: Benchmarking Dyadic Familiarity Inference in Humans and Multimodal Large Language Models
entries.summary: A benchmark for inferring whether two people are already familiar or are meeting as strangers from a 20-second clip of a dyadic ice-breaker conversation, where every pair answers the same prompt so only the manner of interaction reveals the answer. Across text, audio and video, 26 models from seven companies are compared against matched human panels over 96 balanced dyads; the best models match human accuracy but lean toward "stranger", and only humans gain from visible behavior on top of speech.

entries.name: LALM Audio Judge Reliability Assessment
entries.full_title: A Reliability Assessment of LALM Audio Judges for Full-Duplex Voice Agents
entries.summary: An empirical reliability study of Gemini-family models used as audio judges that score full-duplex agent conversations directly from raw stereo waveforms, across 2.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash and 3.1 Pro. Gemini 2.5 Flash is validated against three calibrated human raters on 209 stereo sessions scored on 8 production dimensions: 152 full-duplex conversations across 13 accent-and-condition strata plus 57 adversarial defect-injected clips. Evidence covers rank correlation versus human-human correlation, within-1-point agreement, and sensitivity to injected defects, and the paper warns that a model swap must be re-validated on calibration rather than assumed from rank correlation.
entries.io: stereo conversation audio in, text ratings out
entries.size: 209 stereo sessions (152 conversations + 57 defect-injected clips), 8 dimensions
entries.note: Rank-ordering transfers across the Gemini family but calibration does not: 3.1 Pro rates several dimensions markedly lower than humans despite comparable rank correlation.

entries.name: LALM Judge Shortcut Audit
entries.full_title: Auditing Protocol-Level Shortcuts in Large Audio Language Model Judges for Speech Evaluation
entries.summary: A diagnostic audit of whether large audio-language models used as speech-evaluation judges actually ground their verdicts in the audio or instead exploit protocol-level shortcuts such as specialist labels or reference data supplied by the evaluation protocol. It probes three common deployment protocols, feature-blueprint judging (audio replaced by a structured text description of acoustic features), reference-conditioned judging, and pairwise A/B comparison, over six judges and four attributes.
entries.io: speech (or a text feature description) in, text judgment out
entries.note: Incorrect specialist labels drop five judges' emotion accuracy to 0.10 or below, and one model often picks the same slot regardless of A/B order swaps, showing aggregate agreement can overstate judge validity.

entries.name: M3-DuplexBench
entries.full_title: M3-DuplexBench: A Multi-Turn, Multilingual, Multidomain Benchmark for Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Models
entries.summary: A multi-turn, multilingual, multidomain benchmark for full-duplex spoken dialogue systems, supporting English and Japanese and covering both casual conversation and multi-turn question answering. Models are evaluated under several dialogue-context settings (single-turn, user-only, and teacher-forced full context) to isolate how dialogue history affects behaviour such as turn-taking, backchannelling and barge-in handling.
entries.note: Reveals model-specific turn-taking characteristics, clear gaps across languages and domains, and mixed effects of dialogue context.

entries.name: PJ-Break / AdvAudio-Prosody
entries.full_title: Prosody-driven Jailbreaks in Audio LLMs: A Controlled Study and Mechanistic Analysis
entries.summary: PJ-Break is a black-box evaluation protocol that holds transcript content fixed and varies six speech-delivery presets targeting arousal, authority, and speaking rate, released with AdvAudio-Prosody, a 600-sample benchmark with acoustically verified attributes. On Qwen2-Audio, Panic (38/95), Anger (35/95), and Fast (32/95) presets far exceed Neutral (4/95), and the fixed six-query pool covers 44/95 Qwen2-Audio seeds and 15/95 GPT-4o seeds. Ablations show emotional-delivery audio alone (44/95) is far more effective than emotional text alone (11/95).
entries.venue: Proceedings of the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26), November 10-1

entries.name: RW-Voice-EQ Bench
entries.full_title: RW-Voice-EQ Bench: A Real World Benchmark for Evaluating Voice AI Systems
entries.summary: A multidimensional real-world benchmark that tests whether voice AI systems actually exploit the acoustic information distinguishing speech from text, spanning text-to-speech, speech-to-speech, speech understanding and automatic speech recognition. Results are reported as a profile of dimension-specific capabilities rather than a single aggregate score: for TTS, naturalness, expressiveness, identity stability and reliability behave as largely independent dimensions; for STS, some agents remain transcript-driven despite having audio access; for SU, performance is uneven across paralinguistic tasks; and for ASR, real-world accent, emotion, noise and conversational conditions expose failures that clean-speech benchmarks miss.
entries.io: speech in, speech out (also TTS and ASR tracks)
entries.note: Access to audio does not guarantee use of vocal affect: some speech-to-speech agents remain largely transcript-driven.

entries.name: Sound Symbolism Perceptual Alignment Evaluation
entries.full_title: Hearing Like Humans? Sound Symbolism and Perceptual Alignment in Speech Language Models
entries.summary: An evaluation of whether speech language models share the human tendency of sound symbolism, mapping speech sounds to perceptual qualities such as roundness or sharpness. Unlike prior work that used text or images, it uses genuine human speech recordings and compares model judgments against human data across the auditory, crossmodal and visual components of the effect, with a visual-only control ruling out shape perception as the cause of failure.
entries.note: Model auditory judgments align poorly with human perception and miss acoustic cues such as spectral tilt, localising the weakness to how speech is represented rather than to vision.

entries.name: SPEARBench
entries.full_title: SPEARBench: A Benchmark for Naturalness Evaluation in Streaming Speech-to-Speech Language Models
entries.summary: A benchmark for conversational naturalness of streaming speech-to-speech language models, built from controlled dialogue prompts derived from the Seamless Interaction corpus. Generated answers are scored with a multidimensional protocol covering response latency, interruptions, speech quality, ASR robustness, language and dialect consistency, emotional naturalness, interpersonal stance, and explainable distributional baselines, with original human answers included as a reference condition.
entries.note: Models reach high signal-level quality and low ASR error yet still diverge from human conversational behaviour in latency, overlap, dialect preservation, emotional adaptation and stance dynamics.

entries.name: TurnNat
entries.full_title: TurnNat: Automatic Evaluation of Turn-Taking Naturalness in Dyadic Spoken Dialogue
entries.summary: A likelihood-based framework for automatically evaluating turn-taking naturalness in two-channel spoken dialogue. A causal turn-taking prediction model trained on natural conversations estimates future two-speaker voice-activity states, and the negative log-likelihood of the observed future activity measures timing atypicality; frame-level scores are pooled over turn-taking boundary units and aggregated into a dialogue-level naturalness score. The paper also builds a controlled perturbation benchmark of paired natural and perturbed dialogue clips validated by human naturalness judgments.
entries.io: two-channel dialogue speech in, naturalness score out
entries.note: Unifies heterogeneous timing failures under one reference-free score instead of behaviour-specific timing metrics.

entries.name: VAmoS Bench
entries.full_title: VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench
entries.summary: An end-to-end simulation benchmark that measures whether complete voice-agent systems (cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid) resolve a phone call on their own, the contact-centre notion of containment. The agent plays a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank; each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend, roughly one-third applying adversarial pressure, and the agent may call five tools that execute real SQL. A grader checks binary assertions against the full trace of speech plus tool invocations, arguments and returned rows, catching agents that claim a change they never made or that disclose protected information.
entries.note: Grades against the complete conversation-plus-tool trace, so an agent that claims a card change without updating the database is caught.

entries.name: ARENA
entries.full_title: ARENA: Automated Red-Teaming for Large Audio Language Models
entries.summary: A closed-loop automated red-teaming framework for large audio-language models in the audio-grounded setting, where the text query stays safe in isolation but the joint text-audio input induces harmful behaviour. A controller is trained on an independent 2,000-case text-audio dataset with MD-Judge providing training rewards and adaptive search feedback, while a separate non-adaptive Llama Guard 3 evaluator labels final outcomes, and it is tested on 520 held-out AdvBench objectives.
entries.io: audio plus text in, text out
entries.note: Reaches 87.9/100.0% FDR/PSR on Audio Flamingo 3 and high rates on Qwen2-Audio, MiMo-Audio and GPT-Audio, with feedback refinement and audio-variant search driving the gains.

entries.name: C3PO
entries.full_title: C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models
entries.summary: A benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image and text that evaluates omnimodal models on two abilities: information composition, fusing evidence dispersed across modalities, and counterfactual conflict, resolving deliberate contradictions between modalities. Its paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design, generated by an automatic pipeline from 25 logically grounded templates, are meant to diagnose when and why cross-modal reasoning fails, and attention probes are used to attribute failures to modality dominance.
entries.io: video, audio, image and text in, text out
entries.note: Humans score 88.64% versus 73.17% for the best model, and 86-95% of failures trace to modality dominance with 87-95% of attention on text.

entries.name: Counterfactual audits for paralinguistic response evaluation
entries.full_title: Do Audio Language Models Use Paralinguistic Evidence? Counterfactual Audits for Response Evaluation
entries.summary: An evaluation suite of counterfactual audit items that hold the transcript fixed while varying affect, prosody, or the timing of an affective shift, forcing a valid audio-language-model judge to track the audio cue rather than lexical content or response style. It uses a native one-context judgment protocol plus a contrastive recoverability control and decomposes each item into perception and response-mapping skills to produce diagnostic states for judge failures.

entries.name: DuplexWorld
entries.full_title: DuplexWorld: Can voice agents help you get through the day?
entries.summary: A holistic benchmark for speech-to-speech voice agents across six worlds where such agents are useful (banking, insurance, travel, healthcare, logistics and Pathfinding), aiming beyond tool-calling-against-a-database evaluations to the diversity of everyday conversation and to tasks that are not database manipulation. Agents are evaluated on eleven conversation types across 156 scenarios and over 350 hours of conversation, using agentic, conversational and speech-naturalness metrics, with analysis of agentic versus conversational performance, per-world and per-conversation-type results, failure modes and reliability.
entries.note: Even the best voice agents leave large headroom on all three axes (Pass@1 0.490, turn-taking 0.653, DNSMOS 3.378).

entries.name: EmoSBench
entries.full_title: EmoS: A Theory-Grounded Framework for Evaluating and Aligning Emotional Intelligence in Spoken Language Models
entries.summary: An emotional-intelligence benchmark for spoken language models built on the four-branch theoretical model of emotional intelligence, covering Perceiving, Understanding, Using and Managing Emotion across ten sub-tasks. The paper additionally trains EmoS, a specialised evaluator model fine-tuned with SFT and GRPO on a bilingual dataset (EmoDialogue) of response pairs with defined EI gradations, using rewards for ordinal-score accuracy and rationale fidelity.
entries.note: GPT-4o-Audio reaches only 52.6% on the benchmark, far below the human baseline, while the trained EmoS evaluator reaches 83.8%.

entries.name: FormVoiceAgentBench
entries.full_title: FormBharo: Designing and Evaluating a Voice Agent for Conversational Form Filling in Rural India
entries.summary: An openly released benchmark accompanying FormBharo, a Hindi voice agent that fills structured forms over a phone call. It pairs human-recorded Hindi audio with 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests across 960 simulated calls to evaluate the agent's components (transcription, extraction, reply generation) and end-to-end form completion under real acoustic variations; form completion drops by up to about 41 points when the LLM receives degraded input.
tasks: end-to-end task completion under acoustic noise
entries.size: 3,760 multi-turn conversation tests across 960 simulated calls

entries.name: Hear2Act
entries.full_title: Hear2Act: Benchmarking When Prosody Should Change What an Assistant Does
entries.summary: A unified evaluation protocol for text and spoken assistants that tests whether prosodic evidence actually changes downstream decisions, not just whether it is perceived. It uses 480 persona-grounded task-oriented scenarios with hidden user concerns and objectively verifiable outcomes; the task and user needs are held fixed while the same concern is conveyed either explicitly in words or primarily through prosody, and decisions are evaluated under transcript access, audio access and ground-truth concern-state access.
entries.io: speech in, text out (transcript-only condition included)
entries.note: Adding audio to the transcript barely helps under prosody-mediated feedback (14.6% to 15.3%), but making the model infer the concern into an explicit text state raises the optimal-solution rate to 39.6%, near the 40.7% ground-truth-state ceiling.

entries.name: INSPIRE
entries.full_title: INSPIRE: A Benchmark for Instruction-Aware Speech Retrieval
entries.summary: A benchmark for instruction-aware speech retrieval, in which natural-language instructions dynamically specify the relevance criteria rather than relying on fixed similarity matching. Relevance criteria span semantic content, speaker identity, speaking style, environmental sounds and their combinations, and four retrieval paradigms are compared: large audio-language models, cascaded pipelines, self-supervised speech models, and contrastive audio-language models.
entries.io: speech plus a text instruction in, retrieved speech out
entries.note: No paradigm handles all intents: text-based approaches win on semantics but miss paralinguistic attributes, while speech-based models capture acoustics but follow instructions poorly.

entries.name: ParaIntent
entries.full_title: Towards More Expressive Spoken LLMs: Fine-Grained Intent Benchmarking and Acoustic-Lexical Decoupled Policy Optimization
entries.summary: A Chinese benchmark for spoken emotional dialogue that separates communicative intent stated explicitly in lexical content from intent conveyed implicitly through paralinguistic cues, with 14 intent categories and balanced explicit and implicit samples. Its multidimensional evaluation protocol covers intent fulfillment, response quality and emotional expression, and it is tested on both synthetic and human-recorded test sets. The same paper proposes ALPO, an acoustic-lexical decoupled policy-optimization objective that routes separate textual and acoustic advantages to text and speech tokens.
entries.note: Isolates cases where paralinguistic cues complement or contradict the words, which prior spoken-dialogue benchmarks conflate.

entries.name: Semantic-Aware Bias Estimation for LALMs
entries.full_title: Measuring Fairness in Large Audio Language Models via Semantic-Aware Bias Estimation
entries.summary: An evaluation framework for measuring demographic fairness in large audio language models that explicitly controls for confounders in spoken-input settings. It uses mixed-effects regression with sentence-level semantic embeddings of the reference text as covariates and speaker identity as a random effect, extracting the semantic representations from the same LALM under evaluation so that semantic variation is controlled as the model itself perceives it. Experiments cover simulated data and real-world benchmarks.
entries.note: Ignoring semantic and speaker confounders produces spurious fairness findings; controlling for them yields more robust subgroup estimates.

entries.name: SFC-Bench
entries.full_title: Spoken Function Calling: A New Perspective on Spoken Language Understanding for Large Audio Language Models
entries.summary: Introduces Spoken Function Calling (SFC) as a semantic-understanding perspective beyond closed-set SLU, and synthesizes the SFC-Bench dataset with a multi-agent system from a curated suite of spoken functions extended from traditional SLU datasets. LLMs and Large Audio Language Models are evaluated on it, and LALM SFC capability is further enhanced through post-training.

entries.name: SLT 2026 SmartGlasses Challenge
entries.full_title: The SLT 2026 SmartGlasses Challenge: Benchmarking Egocentric Multi-Talker Speech Recognition and Understanding with Audio-Language Models
entries.summary: A shared-task benchmark for egocentric multi-talker speech processing with audio-language models, recorded from a wearer-centred smart-glasses geometry with dynamic acoustics, speaker overlap and spatial ambiguity. Two tracks, Dyadic Dialogue Understanding and Multi-party Meeting Understanding, jointly evaluate time-stamped speaker-attributed ASR and spoken language understanding over a 106-hour four-channel egocentric speech dataset of 714 real-world sessions. The paper describes the tasks, dataset construction, submissions and shared-evaluation findings.
entries.io: multi-channel egocentric audio in, text out
entries.note: Heavy speaker overlap remains the dominant factor hurting speaker-attributed ASR, and paralinguistic acoustic understanding stays hard for current audio-language models in complex SLU settings.

entries.name: ST-OmniQA
entries.full_title: Listen, See and Track: Spatio-Temporal Audio-Visual Sound Event Reasoning for Omni-Modal Language Models
entries.summary: A spatio-temporal audio-visual question-answering benchmark built from panoramic videos paired with synchronized first-order Ambisonics audio of moving sound sources, containing 40K videos and 400K question-answer pairs across four capability levels covering sound-event recognition, direction of arrival, source distance, motion trajectories, and temporally grounded audio-visual reasoning. The paper additionally proposes ST-Omni-R1, which reaches 77.83% average semantic accuracy versus 37.28% for the best evaluated baseline.

entries.name: Tiered Sound-Source Identification Benchmark
entries.full_title: Can Foundation Models Hear What Made That Sound? A Tiered Benchmark of Audio-Language Models and Traditional Classifiers for Closed-Set Sound Source Identification
entries.summary: A closed-set sound-source identification benchmark over 2,242 clips spanning 23 fine-grained classes in 11 categories, comparing eleven methods: five task-aware closed-set LLMs (four Gemini models plus Kimi-Audio-7B-Instruct), four fixed-vocabulary taggers (YAMNet, PANNs, Whisper-AT, SSLAM), a zero-shot audio-text model (CLAP), and an audio-grounded LLM (BAT). Because the methods differ in how they receive the task and how outputs are scored, they are grouped into four evaluation tiers instead of a single leaderboard, with macro precision, recall, F1 and false-negative rate reported per tier, plus per-class confusion matrices and an analysis of Gemini chain-of-thought over 8,968 responses.
entries.note: Best model reaches 85.6% category-level but only 56.7% fine-grained F1, response length does not predict accuracy, and wrong answers are stated confidently 92-100% of the time.

entries.name: UniVerseBench
entries.full_title: UniVerse: Benchmarking and Enhancing LALMs on Culturally Inclusive Low-Resource Music Understanding
entries.summary: A benchmark for culturally inclusive, low-resource music understanding by large audio-language models, targeting folk-music traditions that are resource-scarce and unevenly represented. UniVerseBench contains 5,042 Q&A pairs across more than 38 cultural and linguistic entities, built by an expert-guided but highly automated pipeline. The paper also releases UniVerseSet, a model-generated multi-turn dialogue training set, and studies multimodal imbalance-learning strategies on dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures.
entries.note: Automated data curation plus imbalance-aware training helps, but models still miss fine-grained acoustic features, showing a gap between surface alignment and deep musical comprehension.

entries.name: OmniAssistBench
entries.full_title: OmniAssistBench: Assistant-style Interaction Benchmark for Omni-LLMs
entries.summary: A benchmark for omni-modal LLMs acting as real-time video assistants that guide a user toward a goal, rather than passively answering questions about a clip. User instructions are embedded into the test video as audio (gesture prompts replace speech in the non-audio prompt-following tasks), and the model must decide whether and when to respond at all. To keep interaction paths from diverging, models are given a prior derived from the source video and must guide the user along that exact route; the data was built by reverse-engineering internet videos into multi-turn clips, plus three filmed real-world cases averaging 15 turns. Two tiers cover 7 major tasks and 16 sub-tasks; scoring is an open-ended GPT-5 judge on a 5-point rubric normalized to 100.
tasks: proactive response (deciding whether and when to speak)
entries.io: video with embedded speech prompts in, text out
entries.size: 300 videos / 685 QA pairs / avg 182.25 s per video, incl. 3 filmed real-world cases
entries.note: Gemini-3-Pro leads at 66.4 and the best open-source model, Qwen3-Omni-Instruct, reaches 51.2, both far below the rubric's threshold for a fully valid answer. Reported failure modes: gesture prompts, losing history across multi-turn interaction, mistaking background speech in the video for a new user instruction, and failing to delay a response until the target event. Building the set took over 1000 expert person-hours.

entries.name: MRMAD
entries.full_title: MRMAD: A Multi-Round Multi-Audio Benchmark for Evaluating Acoustic Degradation Perception in Large Audio-Language Models
entries.summary: A benchmark asking whether audio-language models hear how an audio signal is damaged, not what it says. Clean speech, music and sound clips are re-issued at three severity levels under nine degradation types (ambient noise, low-pass and band-pass filtering, MP3 compression, reverberation, echo, neural vocoder artifacts, DSP denoising artifacts, packet loss; music drops echo, sound drops ambient noise and denoising artifacts). Each item is a multi-turn dialogue in which the reference clip arrives in an earlier turn and the degraded clips in later ones, so the model has to carry a hypothesis about quality across turns rather than judge a single file. Three tasks: identify the degradation type (DTI), compare severity between two clips (DSC), and rank several clips by severity (DSR).
entries.io: multi-round multi-audio in, text (multiple-choice label) out
entries.size: 8,400 multiple-choice questions (speech : music : sound = 9 : 8 : 7; DTI : DSC : DSR = 3 : 3 : 1); built from 5,400 speech clips (VCTK, LibriSpeech, HiFi-TTS, LJSpeech; 192 speakers), 4,800 music clips (MUSDB18-HQ, URMP, FMA-small) and 4,200 sound clips (TAU Urban 2019, FSD50K); average audio 9.1 s, average question 73.8 words
entries.note: 18 models were evaluated across LALM, reasoning-LALM and omni families. Most open-source models sit within a few points of chance on all three tasks (chance is 25 / 50 / 25 for DTI / DSC / DSR), while Gemini 3.1 Pro reaches 86.22 / 90.81 / 64.25. Reasoning training does not rescue it: Audio-Reasoner scores below chance on every task, and the Think variants of Audio Flamingo and MiMo-Audio land at or below their instruct counterparts. The authors' diagnostic is that several models score no worse when the first-turn reference audio is deleted, suggesting degradation cues are attenuated before the audio encoder's output reaches the language model.

entries.name: PUMA
entries.full_title: PUMA: A Polish Benchmark for Culturally Grounded Multimodal Understanding
entries.summary: A hand-built Polish benchmark covering audio, images and documents, of which the three audio categories are what the Atlas tracks: Polish ASR, Speech QA over one- to several-minute recordings (comprehension, information extraction, speaker intent and emotion, tied back to Polish cultural knowledge), and Sound & music QA over non-speech recordings of Polish provenance - ambient noise, instruments, animals, jingles, machinery. Scoring is deterministic and rule-based with no LLM judge: each task reports a strict score (all conditions met, with ASR requiring word accuracy above 0.9) alongside a softer partial-credit score. Models that cannot take audio are evaluated as same-family pairs, one member for vision and one for audio.
tasks: speech QA (comprehension, extraction, intent and emotion)
entries.io: audio, image or document plus text in, text out
entries.size: 900 hand-crafted tasks, 100 per category across nine categories; three of the nine (ASR, Speech QA, Sound & music QA) are audio
entries.note: Audio is the weakest modality for nearly every system tested. Sound & music QA is the hardest category in the whole benchmark - the best strict score is 56 (Gemini-3.1-Pro) - and the authors read that as non-speech audio being a low priority for model developers. The OpenAI pairs lose most of their ground to Gemini on the audio columns specifically. On ASR the paper reports Whisper-Large-v3, released in 2023, beating newer open-weight transcription models on Polish, which the authors take as evidence that Open ASR Leaderboard standings on high-resource languages do not transfer to less-resourced ones. Gemini-3.1-Pro leads overall at 79.7 strict. Claude-Fable-5 was run on the vision and document categories only, having no audio support, and Gemma 4's 30-second audio limit ruled it out of the audio categories.

entries.name: EXAM2
entries.full_title: EXAM2: Extending Audio Understanding in Multilingual and Multimodal Analysis
entries.summary: A multiple-choice audio-understanding benchmark that adds two axes existing audio MCQ sets leave fixed: language and visual grounding. Every question and every answer choice is rendered in six languages (English, German, Spanish, Japanese, Malay, Chinese), and every answer choice also carries a generated image, so a model can be scored on audio alone, on images alone, or on both together. Items are rebuilt from four existing corpora rather than recorded fresh: the 998-question test split is a cleaned restructuring of MMAU-test-mini (two music items dropped, duplicate choices removed), and the 4,669-question train split is filtered from MMAR (129 of 1,000 items discarded for dead audio links) and AudioMCQ-Clotho. Translation is by GPT-5-mini with native-speaker or advanced-proficiency review; answer images come from Stable Diffusion (MMAU and MMAR subsets) and GPT-image-2 (Clotho subset), with misleading images manually replaced. The paper also releases OmniLoRA, a LoRA recipe that samples one of the six languages per training instance, and Gemma3n-EXAM2, a fine-tune of Gemma-3n-E4B on EXAM2-train.
tasks: cross-modal MCQ with image answer choices
entries.io: audio (optionally plus one image per answer choice) and text question in, choice index out
entries.size: 5,667 multiple-choice questions total (998 test / 4,669 train), 22,614 image answer choices, 135,684 multilingual question-and-choice instances; average audio 12.9 s, average question 10.7 words
metrics: multiple-choice accuracy (%), reported per audio domain and per language
entries.note: Because every item exists in an audio version, an image version and a transcript or caption version, the paper can put native-audio models and cascaded transcript-fed models on the same questions. The cascade is often the stronger configuration for open-weight models: Qwen-2.5-Omni scores 40.71 average on raw audio but 58.10 when fed a transcript, and Gemma-3n goes from 45.44 to 59.91 the same way, i.e. these models do better on the text of the question than on the sound it describes. GPT-4o-audio leads overall at 73.83. The authors' own Gemma3n-EXAM2 fine-tune reaches 61.24 average, best among open-source entries and best on speech (64.31) and music (60.14), but plain Gemma-3n fed a caption still wins the sound column (67.12 vs 59.26). Caveat worth flagging: the test split is derived from MMAU-test-mini, so scores here are not independent of MMAU.

entries.name: LongAudioQA
entries.full_title: Don't Just Listen, Try Planning: Graph-based Retrieval-Generation Agent for Long-form Audio Meeting Understanding
entries.summary: A question-answering set for long-form meeting audio, built over three existing corpora: AliMeeting (Mandarin far-field meetings), AMI (English far-field meetings with mostly non-native speakers) and DailyTalk (clean dyadic conversations, 20 clips concatenated to reach roughly ten minutes). Recordings average about 32 minutes for the two meeting corpora, so the task is explicitly about answering without knowing which segment holds the evidence. Questions fall into five types: factual retrieval, inferential multi-hop reasoning (causal links, coreference, stance change), temporal (absolute localisation, relative sequencing, frequency counts), summarisation (topic consensus, speaker profiling) and acoustic-aware, the last of which cannot be answered from a transcript because it asks who sounded agitated or why a voice suddenly rose at a given minute. Questions are LLM-generated from localised evidence and then human-verified: hallucinated items discarded, ambiguous references rewritten, hop count checked, and generated timestamp evidence required to reach IoU above 0.9 with ground truth; reported inter-annotator agreement is Cohen's kappa 0.91. Scoring is semantic accuracy judged by GPT-OSS-120B rather than exact match.
entries.io: long-form meeting audio (or its transcript) plus a text question in, free-form text answer out
entries.size: 16,456 question-answer pairs over 190 dialogues and 54.74 hours: AliMeeting 3,013 Q&A / 28 dialogues / 14.91 h, AMI 3,243 / 34 / 18.24 h, DailyTalk 10,200 / 128 / 21.59 h
metrics: human ratings of correctness, coherence and groundedness
entries.note: Introduced alongside a method (GRGA, a graph-based retrieval-generation agent), so every number in the paper comes from the authors of the dataset - treat the baseline column as a first data point, not as an independent leaderboard. The results do isolate one clean effect: end-to-end spoken LLMs given the whole recording as audio collapse on temporal questions (Qwen3-Omni 2.43, Audio Flamingo 3 3.83, MiMo-Audio 5.58 on DailyTalk) while the same models fed the transcript instead score in the 58-63 range, i.e. the failure is context length and time-indexing, not the questions. The reverse holds on the acoustic-aware split, where audio input beats transcript input for Audio Flamingo 3 (40.09 vs 15.85) and MiMo-Audio (31.44 vs 17.52) on DailyTalk. Reported ASR and diarisation error on the underlying audio (WER 18.84-20.38, DER 13.10-17.60 on the two meeting corpora) bounds how much any transcript-based route can recover.

entries.name: TurnBench
entries.full_title: TurnBench: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Turn-Taking Dynamics in Spoken Dialogue
entries.summary: A hand-annotated turn-taking benchmark that scores two boundary-detection tracks against a single consensus annotation of the same conversation: end-of-turn (the floor leaves a speaker) and interruption (a listener takes the floor away from a talking speaker mid-turn). Its point of difference is that conversation type is a controlled variable: 154 dual-channel dyadic dialogues are recorded under six interaction styles (casual, task-oriented, instructional, collaborative, argumentative, narrative), roughly balanced, with each session's style and topic fixed in an unrecorded warm-up and no instruction ever given about turn-taking behaviour itself. Every VAD-segmented span is labelled by three independent annotators from a 17-label inventory collapsed to seven canonical events, and the per-annotator tracks are released so disagreement can be used rather than discarded. A submission is a JSON list of event timestamps per speaker, so continuous-probability systems must pick an operating point; the paper fixes thresholds on the dev split under a 0.1 false-positive budget. Scoring is recall and false-positive rate per track plus median signed latency against the gold boundary. Fourteen heterogeneous systems are compared, from an energy VAD floor through deployed endpointing APIs and trained turn-taking predictors to full-duplex spoken dialogue models, which are evaluated zero-shot by putting the model in the conversation in place of one speaker and reading end-of-turn decisions off its produced audio (interruption is not scored for them). Two findings frame the difficulty: end-of-turn recall is roughly stable across conversation types while interruption false positives are strongly type-dependent and concentrate in backchannel-dense styles, and no system matches the human pattern of starting to speak a median 151 ms before the current turn ends without paying an excessive false-positive cost.
entries.size: ~30 h of dual-channel dyadic speech, 154 dialogues (mean ~11.7 min) from 106 voice actors in 53 pairs; 38-dialogue dev split released with labels, 116-dialogue test split audio-only; separate ~104 h speaker-disjoint training set
entries.note: English, studio-recorded and dyadic by design, and the majority-consensus gold drops events the three annotators disagreed on. Full-duplex spoken dialogue models are scored on end-of-turn only, and their latency includes response generation (and, for hosted models, network delay), so it is not comparable with a predictor's decision latency. Data is under a custom non-commercial licence prohibiting voice cloning. A public leaderboard and dataset viewer are at turnbench.sesame.com.
